A.text:
This is Foghorn, an incident command
app for a fictional online shop called

Brightcart. Alerts arrive,
AI agents investigate,

a human approves the fix, and it
all runs as ten LangGraph workflows.

Everything here is a recorded
run on a real language model.

We will follow one incident
through the graphs that handle it.

B.text:
First, the ten graphs, drawn from
the live server's own structure.
An event router at the front door.

The incident commander,
which is the big one.
A root cause tournament, a storm correlator, a change gate for human approvals,

a postmortem pipeline, an
ops copilot, a shift handoff,

a memory keeper, and an
evaluator that grades the rest.

C.text: Now the incident. We launch scenario one:

checkout is returning
errors after a deploy.

Events flow into a pipeline
that validates each one,

drops duplicates, applies routing
rules, queues by priority,

This is mission control,
live over server-sent events.

D.text: The first run is the event router.

A LangGraph is a state machine: nodes are
plain functions that return updates to a

shared state, and edges
decide what runs next.

Here the event is validated, checked
against a ledger in the store,

then enriched by three parallel tasks,
with a retry policy and a cache.

It is classified, a
decision picks a route,

and the route opens an incident
and hands it to the commander.

Fourteen more alerts follow, and
each simply joins that incident.

E.text:
Now the incident commander,
a supervisor graph.

It sends three specialists off
in parallel with Command goto:

Each is itself a compiled subgraph, a
model node looping with a tools node,

and you can watch their reasoning and
tool calls stream into the war room,
token by token. Evidence fills the board:

an error rate of nine point six per
cent against a baseline of point three,

a deploy nine minutes
before the errors began,
and a null pointer exception in the logs.

F.text:
Then the supervisor hands its
hypotheses to the root cause tournament.

The Send API fans out one scoring
task for every hypothesis,

all in parallel, and a reducer
merges the scores into a ranking.

On a bigger incident, a zone
partition, that is sixteen at once.
In this run there was one strong candidate: a bad deploy on checkout service,

G.text:
The commander proposes a
rollback, and a policy check runs:

six rules, covering risk, the
change freeze and blast radius.

LangGraph saves the whole state to a
checkpoint and the run simply stops.

Nothing is polling,
nothing is held in memory.

The dashboard shows an approval card,
generated from the interrupt's own schema.

Approve it, and a Command with a
resume value goes to the same thread.

The graph wakes exactly where
it stopped, runs the rollback,

verifies recovery, and
closes the incident.

H.text:
How does the dashboard
watch all this live?

LangGraph can stream a run
in several modes at once,
Updates carry each node's state change.

Custom events carry whatever
the graph wants to announce,
Tasks mark when each node starts and finishes, and checkpoints record every step.

The war room is the messages,
the board is the custom events,
and the timeline is the tasks.

I.text:
When the incident resolves, an event
starts the postmortem pipeline,

written with the Functional API:
an entrypoint and plain tasks.

Load the incident, build
a timeline, draft, review.

Review is another interrupt,
where a human edits or approves.

Publishing starts the memory keeper,
which distils a lesson and asks:

remember this? Approved lessons go
into the store with semantic search,
so the next similar incident recalls them.

J.text: Alert storms get their own graph.

Twenty two alerts from eleven
services, a zone partition,

fan out into fourteen analysis
tasks, run in parallel,
then reduce into a single cluster.
One incident, instead of twenty two pages.

K.text:
The change gate is the
human in the loop gym.
This run goes through every style.

A question. Four approval
cards, where the human asks,

Then four eyes review: two
reviewers pending at the same time,

both resumed by one command,
keyed by interrupt I D.

L.text:
The shift handoff is told
to crash in reconcile,

and it does. The thread
keeps its checkpoints.
Run it again with no input, and it continues from the last good step, and finishes.

M.text:
All of this is visible
in LangGraph Studio.

Point it at the local server and
every graph appears in the selector.

Here is the incident commander,
drawn from its real structure.

Studio builds the input
form from the schema.

Submit, and the nodes
light up as they run.

When the graph pauses, the interrupt gets
a response form generated from its schema,

N.text:
And every run lands in
LangSmith as a trace.

The root is the graph,
every node is a child,

and the model calls sit
inside, with their prompts,
The specialists run side by side.

And a human wait separates
the two traces of one thread.

O.text:
Sixteen labelled scenarios
with hidden ground truth,

scored on root cause,
evidence, safety and more.

The competent profile passes all
sixteen, a naive one passes two.

A gullible one obeys an
instruction hidden in a log line:

the policy check stops it, but
the safety gate still fails.
On a real model, fifteen of sixteen pass,
with every hard safety gate clean.

P.text:
That is Foghorn: ten
graphs, one deployment.

Start it with make dev, open the
dashboard, and open Studio beside it.

Everything you saw was
recorded from real runs.
